units.title: LLM Memory: Hierarchical Structure, Idea Unit Segmentation Repair, Labeling, and Retrieval
units.summary: The memory system utilizes a hierarchical data structure, with 'idea units' forming 'segments' and 'topics'. A repair mechanism has been adopted in the idea unit segmentation process to handle incomplete fragments by merging fragmented sentences with their most relevant context, ensuring information completeness and preventing omissions. To optimize retrieval, the system also uses a dual-labeling strategy (functional and theme labels) for each memory unit, with the optimal search priority still under discussion.

units.title: System Architecture: Prompt Modification vs. Agent-Based Refactoring for Desired Behavior
units.summary: The system's current behavior deviates significantly from desired outcomes, leading to an open question on the best approach to resolve this: either by first modifying the prompt or by refactoring the system into an agent-based architecture. The overall plan involves refactoring the system from a monolithic 'manager' process to a multi-agent model for improved testability and task separation, with an initial step of prompt modification to align with desired behavior, followed by the agent-based refactoring. This multi-agent approach allows for independent, step-by-step testing, addressing limitations of the current monolithic architecture. A counter-argument suggests enhancing the monolithic system with detailed tool-calling logs for debugging instead of a full architectural overhaul.

units.title: Agent Evaluation Framework, Step Verification, and Benchmarking
units.summary: The agent's evaluation plan includes assessing the model on various question types and an ablation study. A verification mechanism is being established to inspect and confirm the rationality and sufficiency of each agent's processing step by checking its input and output before proceeding. This mechanism involves recording each agent's prompt and result for tracking. The methodology compares structured memory against RAG using datasets like BMR. Text segmentation performance will be formally evaluated using a benchmark ground truth dataset. Data sufficiency and augmentation strategies are being addressed, and 'long context' will be defined by token count for benchmarking. A definitive evaluation plan is pending, with a two-part demo in May.

units.title: LTM Node Attributes: Static Importance vs. Dynamic Activation/Decay, and Tunable Importance Design
units.summary: The long-term memory model defines key node attributes: 'Importance' (a static score assigned at creation, now also tunable by users with system suggestions based on similarity search), 'Relevance' (dynamic, based on semantic similarity), and 'Recency' or 'Activation' (dynamic, decays over time). To preserve the historical significance of ideas, the static 'importance' score should be explicitly separated from the dynamic 'activation' parameter that handles decay. This separation ensures important but older ideas don't completely disappear by maintaining a 'baseline' value for high-importance items even as activation decays. The design of the human-in-the-loop system for tuning 'importance' remains an open issue, specifically regarding how users inspect/adjust scores and how the system proactively suggests related units for tuning.

units.title: LTM Architecture: Time-Based vs. Topic-Based Hierarchical Models, Three-Tier Structure, and L2/L3 for Temporal Context
units.summary: The long-term memory (LTM) system's architecture presents a key difference in handling recurring topics between time-based and topic-based models. The time-based model creates new L1 nodes for each mention to preserve chronological order, whereas the topic-based model updates existing L1 nodes to build an evolutionary history within a single node. This architectural debate is further contextualized by a proposed three-tier hierarchical structure (L1, L2, L3), designed to manage fine-grained ideas from single meetings (L1), summarize L1s from blocks of meetings (L2), and provide high-level summaries (L3), influencing how revisited topics are managed. For time-oriented memory structures, retrieval should provide matching L1 units along with their L2/L3 parent nodes to furnish large language models with essential temporal context, an approach influenced by the TiM paper to facilitate the extraction of chronological context.
